data.title: Infantile haemangioma & vascular malformations — viva
data.summary: Vascular & ulcers · 12 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Infantile haemangioma & vascular malformations** (Vascular & ulcers)_

**Q1. Give the ISSVA classification of vascular anomalies.**
- Vascular tumours (endothelial proliferation): benign — infantile haemangioma, congenital haemangioma (RICH, NICH, PICH), tufted angioma, spindle-cell haemangioma, pyogenic granuloma; locally aggressive/borderline — kaposiform haemangioendothelioma, Kaposi sarcoma; malignant — angiosarcoma
- Vascular malformations (errors of morphogenesis, no proliferation): simple — capillary (CM, port-wine stain), venous (VM), lymphatic (LM — macro/microcystic), arteriovenous (AVM, high flow), AV fistula; combined (CVM, CLVM, CLAVM); of major named vessels; associated with other anomalies (Sturge–Weber, Klippel–Trenaunay, Parkes Weber, Proteus, CLOVES, Maffucci, PROS)

**Q2. Differentiate infantile haemangioma from vascular malformation.**
- Haemangioma: usually absent or a premonitory mark at birth; appears in first weeks; rapid proliferation till 3–5 months (80% of final size), slow involution over years; GLUT-1 positive; female, premature, low birth weight, multiple gestation, placental anomalies
- Malformation: present at birth (may be inapparent), grows proportionately with the child, never involutes, may enlarge with trauma, infection, hormones; GLUT-1 negative; flow characteristics on Doppler (slow vs fast flow)

**Q3. Describe clinical types of infantile haemangioma.**
- Superficial (bright red, lobulated 'strawberry'), deep (bluish subcutaneous swelling), mixed
- Pattern: focal, segmental (plaque in a developmental segment — more complications), indeterminate, multifocal (≥5 lesions — screen for hepatic haemangiomas with ultrasound)
- Abortive/minimal-growth haemangioma (telangiectatic patch, lower body)

**Q4. Which haemangiomas are high-risk and need treatment?**
- Life-threatening: airway ('beard area' segmental — subglottic), liver (high-output cardiac failure, hypothyroidism), large lesions with cardiac failure
- Functional impairment: periocular (amblyopia, astigmatism), lip, nasal tip, ear canal, feeding problems
- Ulceration (commonest complication — lip, anogenital, flexures; painful, scarring)
- Disfigurement: central face, large facial, nose ('Cyrano'), breast in girls
- Associated syndromes: PHACE (Posterior fossa anomalies, Haemangioma (large segmental facial), Arterial anomalies, Cardiac defects/coarctation, Eye anomalies, ± sternal cleft/supraumbilical raphe); LUMBAR/SACRAL/PELVIS (lumbosacral haemangioma with spinal dysraphism, genitourinary, anorectal anomalies — do spine USG/MRI)

**Q5. Treatment of infantile haemangioma.**
- Oral propranolol — first line for high-risk lesions: 1 mg/kg/day increasing to 2–3 mg/kg/day in 2–3 divided doses with feeds, start ideally by 1–2 months of age (before 5 months), continue till ~12 months of age (6 months minimum); baseline examination (heart rate, BP, ± ECG if bradycardia/heart disease), side effects — hypoglycaemia (feed regularly; stop if not feeding), bronchospasm, bradycardia, hypotension, sleep disturbance, cold extremities; rebound growth on stopping
- Atenolol (fewer CNS effects) and nadolol as alternatives
- Topical timolol 0.5% gel for small superficial lesions
- Systemic/intralesional steroids (second line), vincristine, sirolimus (kaposiform)
- Pulsed-dye laser for ulceration and residual telangiectasia; surgery for fibrofatty residue after involution
- Ulcer care: barrier creams, dressings, topical antibiotics, propranolol

**Q6. Mechanism of propranolol in haemangiomas.**
- Vasoconstriction (early colour change), inhibition of VEGF and bFGF (angiogenesis), induction of apoptosis of endothelial cells, effects on haemangioma stem cells and renin–angiotensin system

**Q7. What is Kasabach–Merritt phenomenon?**
- Profound thrombocytopenia and consumptive coagulopathy due to platelet trapping in kaposiform haemangioendothelioma or tufted angioma (NOT infantile haemangioma)
- Rapidly enlarging, firm, purpuric/ecchymotic mass in infancy; treat with sirolimus, vincristine, steroids; avoid platelet transfusion unless bleeding

**Q8. Describe port-wine stain and Sturge–Weber syndrome.**
- Port-wine stain (capillary malformation): pink-red macular patch present at birth, persists, darkens and thickens with age (nodularity — 'cobblestoning'), soft-tissue hypertrophy; somatic GNAQ mutation
- Sturge–Weber: facial CM in V1 (forehead/upper eyelid) distribution + ipsilateral leptomeningeal angiomatosis (seizures, hemiparesis, intellectual disability, tram-track calcification on imaging) + eye (glaucoma, choroidal haemangioma)
- Treatment of PWS: pulsed-dye laser (585/595 nm) early in infancy — best results; topical rapamycin adjunct; MRI brain and eye check for V1 lesions

**Q9. What is Klippel–Trenaunay syndrome? (PYQ)**
- Capillary–lymphatic–venous malformation of a limb (usually lower) + soft-tissue and bone overgrowth (limb hypertrophy) + varicosities/persistent embryonic lateral marginal vein (vein of Servelle) — slow flow; PIK3CA mutation (PROS spectrum)
- Complications: DVT/pulmonary embolism, bleeding, lymphatic leaks, cellulitis, limb-length discrepancy, coagulopathy
- Parkes Weber syndrome — similar but with arteriovenous fistulas (fast flow; RASA1) — high-output cardiac failure
- Management: compression, sclerotherapy, sirolimus, alpelisib (PIK3CA inhibitor), orthopaedic correction, anticoagulation when indicated

**Q10. Write a short note on blue rubber bleb naevus syndrome (PYQ).**
- Multifocal venous malformations of skin (soft, compressible blue rubbery nodules that refill after pressure, may be painful/sweat) and GI tract (bleeding → iron-deficiency anaemia); TEK (TIE2) somatic mutations
- Treatment: iron, endoscopic ablation/resection of bleeding lesions, sirolimus

**Q11. Enumerate syndromes associated with vascular anomalies (PYQ).**
- Sturge–Weber, Klippel–Trenaunay, Parkes Weber, Proteus, CLOVES, PHACE, LUMBAR, Maffucci (enchondromas + spindle-cell haemangiomas; risk of chondrosarcoma), blue rubber bleb, Cobb (spinal AVM + cutaneous vascular lesion in dermatome), von Hippel–Lindau, hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler–Weber–Rendu — epistaxis, mucocutaneous telangiectasia, AVMs; ENG/ACVRL1), ataxia-telangiectasia, capillary malformation–AVM (RASA1), macrocephaly–capillary malformation (M-CM), Beckwith–Wiedemann (glabellar naevus flammeus)

**Q12. Lasers for vascular lesions (PYQ).**
- Selective photothermolysis targeting oxyhaemoglobin (peaks 418, 542, 577 nm): pulsed-dye laser 585/595 nm (port-wine stain, haemangioma, telangiectasia, rosacea), KTP 532 nm, long-pulsed Nd:YAG 1064 nm (deeper veins, leg veins), IPL, alexandrite 755 nm (hypertrophic PWS)
- Side effects: purpura, dyspigmentation, blistering, scarring

## Quick spotter facts
- Absent at birth, grows fast, then involutes, GLUT-1+ — infantile haemangioma
- Propranolol 2–3 mg/kg/day
- V1 port-wine stain — look for Sturge–Weber; KMP is with kaposiform HE, not infantile haemangioma

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Vascular anomalies); ISSVA 2018 classification. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
